title: India Weighs Mandatory Annual Drug Tests for All Pilots After Air India Marijuana Incident
excerpt: Civil Aviation Minister says DGCA is consulting stakeholders on expanding pilot drug testing from 10 percent to 100 percent of the workforce annually.
body:
• India's Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu said the DGCA is considering mandatory drug tests for every commercial pilot at least once a year at a random time.
  • Current regulations require airlines to test only 10% of their pilot network annually, a threshold many experts consider insufficient.
  • The proposal follows an Air India pilot testing positive for marijuana after a Phuket-Delhi flight on August 4 that saw a sudden 300-foot altitude loss, injuring 17 people.
  • The Federation of Indian Pilots has urged expanding random testing to 20-25% and adopting faster oral fluid tests alongside urine testing to minimize flight delays.

From 10 Percent to 100 Percent

India's aviation regulator is evaluating a sweeping expansion of drug testing for commercial pilots, with the government floating a proposal to test every pilot in the country at least once a year at a randomly selected time.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=ZqhsfzYX7II

Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu told reporters in New Delhi that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is actively consulting stakeholders on the plan. "Right now, the rule says 10 percent across the overall pilot network. The DGCA is engaging and one of the opinions from our side is that everyone has to go through it in the year at a random time," Naidu said.

The minister acknowledged that the government must weigh competing priorities. "We have to see how all the stakeholders are going to respond to this because one is the safety aspect of it and the second thing is the operational impact, which also has to be taken into consideration," he said.

The Incident That Triggered the Review

The policy review was prompted by an August 4 incident involving Air India flight AI2379, an Airbus A320 operating from Phuket to Delhi. The aircraft experienced a sudden loss of approximately 300 feet of altitude during cruise after a hydraulic failure before stabilizing and landing safely in Delhi. At least 17 people, including cabin crew members, were injured.

Both pilots underwent mandatory psychoactive substance screening after landing. The pilot-in-command's initial screening returned "non-negative," and a confirmatory drug test subsequently came back positive for marijuana, according to multiple media reports. The DGCA took both pilots off the roster pending investigation, and the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) classified the drop as a "serious incident."

"No inference regarding the cause of the occurrence should be drawn from any isolated piece of information while the investigation is in progress."

— Ministry of Civil Aviation statement

Air India subsequently expanded drug screening across its pilot workforce. Air India and Air India Express screened approximately 5,000 pilots in a one-time exercise, with two returning non-negative initial results, according to India Today.

Industry Pushback on Logistics

Aviation experts and pilot unions have raised concerns about the feasibility of 100 percent testing. On India Today's NewsTrack, experts highlighted major logistical hurdles including a shortage of certified testing laboratories, high implementation costs, and the risk of flight disruptions or temporary pilot shortages.

The Federation of Indian Pilots (FIP) has advocated a middle ground. FIP President Captain CS Randhawa urged increasing random testing coverage to 20-25 percent of pilots annually, rather than jumping to full coverage. The federation has also pushed for adopting oral fluid swab testing alongside traditional urine tests, arguing that the faster turnaround would minimize pilot downtime and reduce the operational impact on flight schedules.

Implications for Travelers

For the millions of passengers who fly Indian carriers each year — including the substantial traffic on India-US routes operated by Air India — the proposed changes represent a significant tightening of safety oversight. India's commercial aviation sector has grown rapidly, and the country's airlines now operate one of the world's largest domestic networks.

The DGCA is also conducting separate stakeholder consultations on the broader regulatory framework governing substance use among pilots, Naidu said. These discussions are running independently of the ongoing AAIB investigation into the August 4 incident.

What's Next

The AAIB is examining the flight data recorder and other aircraft systems from the Air India flight, with a preliminary report expected soon. A final decision on expanding the testing regime will come after the DGCA completes its stakeholder consultations and assesses the balance between enhanced safety enforcement and operational viability across India's airline industry.
